title: Practicing Good with a Sincere Heart
excerpt: Translation: The coming of misfortune and blessing has no other cause than what one’s own thoughts and actions summon forth. The retribution of good and evil from one’s thoughts and actions is like a shadow following the body and moving in accord with it—do evil and misfortune comes; do good and blessing comes.

inline.s: Misfortune and blessing have no door of their own—only people summon them;
The retribution of good and evil follows like a shadow the form.

The coming of misfortune and blessing has no other cause than what one’s own thoughts and actions summon forth. The retribution of good and evil from one’s thoughts and actions is like a shadow following the body and moving in accord with it—do evil and misfortune comes; do good and blessing comes.

In the Ming dynasty there was a Minister of Justice, Liu by name, who harbored a heart of benevolence and forgiveness, upheld the law impartially, and was never harsh. His son Liu Jing (jǐng) was extremely frail and often ill. He had had five elder brothers, all of whom had died young. The Minister, seeing this only remaining sixth son so sickly, was greatly worried. Whenever he met a physiognomist or fortune-teller he would ask them to calculate Liu Jing’s fate; but unfortunately most said that Liu Jing would meet a great calamity at nineteen, and so his father grew the more anxious. Just then a physiognomist from Sichuan, Zhou Tulian by name, came to visit the capital; his readings of people’s faces were extremely accurate, and his reputation resounded throughout the capital. The Minister therefore invited Zhou Tulian to his home and asked him to read Liu Jing’s lifelong fortune and lifespan.
[Lu: the emolument of officials in ancient times; also used by extension to mean wealth and rank.]

After gazing for a long while, the physiognomist Zhou said: “As to the young master’s lifespan, I fear it will be hard to get past the barrier of nineteen. But on no account should you lose heart over this; you must know that ‘though the span of life is decreed by Heaven, the establishment of life lies within ourselves.’ In general, a person’s measure of rank and lifespan is bound up with the good or evil karma created in past lives. The Sutra of the Original Vows of Earth Store Bodhisattva says that those who in a past life killed living beings must in this life receive the retribution of a short life. On this reckoning, the young master’s karma of killing in a former life must be heavy. Since we know the cause of the short-life appearance, there is a method to remedy it. By refraining from killing and releasing living beings, and extensively cultivating all kinds of good karma to make up for it, it is not difficult to exchange a short life for a long one. It is like a sick person whose illness has already been diagnosed: so long as the medicine meets the disease, one will swiftly recover. But as to cultivating good, one must do it with all one’s heart and strength. Only when the good karma of this life far surpasses the evil karma of past lives can a real effect be obtained. If the young master’s past-life evil karma amounts to eight parts, then in this life, repenting of evil and cultivating good, one must reach ten parts before one can make good and recover the rank and lifespan fixed by fate. If one attains only six or seven parts, or barely manages eight, then good will not overcome evil; this is like a grave illness treated with too little medicine, hard to revive the dying, and I fear an immediate effect will be hard to see. But this is not to say that doing good comes to nothing; these good deeds are still useful for planting good roots in a future life. People often see many who do good or evil without any obvious retribution and so doubt that Heaven is without awareness; this is because the fleshly eye cannot see the threefold cause and effect of past, present, and future, nor the relative strength of past karma. I earnestly beg the honored father and son to believe the Buddha’s words, which are real and not false. If you act with utmost sincerity, the young master is sure to enjoy fortune and a long life—there is no need to worry.” He then instructed them to uphold the Most High’s Tract on Actions and Responses and to practice it unrelentingly without letting up.

At this time Liu Jing was barely seventeen, gifted and intelligent, and very able to spur himself on. Hearing the physiognomist’s words, he took them as maxims of truth and made a vow to Heaven, resolving to uphold the Most High’s Tract on Actions and Responses, to abandon evil and cultivate good. He copied out the items of good and evil in the tract one by one. The good ones he pasted on the east wall, adding a red circle for every good act done; the evil ones on the west wall, adding a black circle for every offense committed. Even for a single arising thought he strictly reproved himself, not daring to excuse himself. In refraining from killing and releasing living beings he was especially diligent, never the least remiss. In this way he practiced for three years and was able to pass the barrier of nineteen in safety.

One day, on some business, he crossed the Yangtze by boat and saw a fisherman netting a very large turtle. Liu Jing’s compassionate heart was stirred, and he ordered his attendant to give a thousand coins to buy it and set it free. Strangely, once put into the water the turtle seemed to have intelligence; it raised its head and nodded, then followed behind Liu Jing’s boat, escorting him for five li, and when Liu Jing came ashore it still lingered, unwilling to leave. That night, in a hostel, Liu Jing dreamed that a dark-robed, short, stocky Daoist said to him: ‘The young master has practiced the Tract for three years without ever growing weary; the Heavenly Emperor very much commends you, and you have already been granted increased fortune and a longer life. But your constitution is frail, and one cannot be sure that heat and cold will not harm you. The humble priest has a small method to teach you; by following it to regulate the body and nurture yourself, you may keep your body well and free of illness.’ Having said this, he passed on to him the method of regulating the breath to ward off illness.

When Liu Jing awoke, he knew the divine turtle had repaid his kindness, and from then on practiced according to the method and indeed grew healthier day by day. Later the Minister again invited Zhou Tulian to his home to thank him for his former guidance. That night Zhou lay on the same bed as Liu Jing, and waking at midnight saw Liu Jing in deep sleep with no the faintest breath; feeling his body, it was as if he were dead. The next morning he rose and congratulated the Minister: “In the few years since we parted, the young master’s bone-structure has changed greatly from before. Regarding him in sleep, he has already received the transmission of the turtle’s breath. Not only will his health be sound and his years long, but his later fortune will reach far without limit. This is truly the blessing of the honored father and son practicing good with a sincere heart.” Later Liu Jing lived to ninety-eight, and his descendants were worthy and accomplished, with both fortune and longevity complete—exactly as Zhou Tulian had foretold.
